## About

This repository contains the official distroless images for Azure Linux. Azure Linux distroless container images are lightweight and provide a minimal attack surface. The 3 primary distroless images are labelled: `minimal`, `base`, and `debug`. If you are familiar with the Google distroless container images, these are equivalent to their `static`, `base`, and `base-debug` images, respectively.

### What is Azure Linux?

Azure Linux is a Linux distribution for Microsoft’s cloud infrastructure and edge products and services. Azure Linux is designed to provide a consistent platform for these devices and services and will enhance Microsoft’s ability to stay current on Linux updates.  

To learn more about Azure Linux, refer to our [GitHub repository](https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/).

### What is a distroless container?

Distroless containers contain only the minimal set of packages your application needs, with anything extra removed (i.e. package manager, libraries and shell). Both Qualys and Trivy support vulnerability scanning in Azure Linux distroless containers.

Due to their limited set of packages, distroless containers have a minimized security attack surface as well as reduced noise from vulnerability scanners. This generally translates to a reduced overhead of patching vulnerabilities, allowing developers to focus on building their application. Lastly, the smaller size (~10MB) provides higher performance.

## Featured tags

- `3.0`

### What images are available?

| Image             | Tags     |
| ----------------- | -------- |
| `mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/minimal` | `3.0` |
| `mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/base`    | `3.0` |
| `mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/debug`   | `3.0` |

### Minimal
The `minimal` image is the smallest distroless image. It includes the following Azure Linux packages and is primarily intended for use with golang or other statically linked applications:

| Package                   | Description       |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `filesystem`              | folder layout     |
| `azurelinux-release`      | Azure Linux version info |
| `prebuilt-ca-certificates`| prebuilt version of the ca-certificates package with no runtime dependencies |
| `tzdata`                  | timezone data     |

### Base
The `base` image adds the following Azure Linux packages to the `minimal` image and is primarily intended for C based applications:

| Package                   | Description       |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `glibc`                   | main C library    |
| `glibc-iconv`             | gconv modules for glibc |
| `iana-etc`                | networking data   |
| `libgcc`                  | GNU C Library |
| `openssl`                 | utilities from general purpose cryptography library with TLS implementation |
| `openssl-libs`            | general purpose cryptography library with TLS implementation |
| `SymCrypt`                | core cryptographic library written by Microsoft |
| `SymCrypt-OpenSSL`        | SymCrypt engine for OpenSSL (SCOSSL) allows the use of OpenSSL with SymCrypt as the provider for core cryptographic operations |

### Debug
The `debug` image adds the following packages to the `base` image and provides a lightweight debugging environment:

| Package                   | Description       |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `busybox`                 | contains `/usr/sbin/busybox` and minimal versions of various GNU utilities |

The distroless debug image has a busybox shell. You can launch this shell by running the following command:

    docker run -it --rm mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/debug:3.0 busybox sh

Once inside the shell, you can then run the following command to get a list of available functions:

    busybox

An example command to list the current directory would be

    busybox ls

TIP: If you'd like to run shell commands directly without typing busybox everytime (e.g., `/ # ls` as opposed to `/ # busybox ls`) , you can run the following command to "install" busybox:

    busybox --install -s

For more information on busybox, please refer to this document: https://www.busybox.net/.

## Configuration

#### Docker multi-stage build

Using Docker’s multi-stage build provides an easy way to use distroless images. The basic idea is that you'll have one stage to build your application artifacts or install additional packages and insert them into your runtime distroless image. To learn more, please see the documentation on [multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/multistage-build/).

Below is an example of how to create and run a Node.js Distroless container. The aim of this example is to show how to create a distroless container for a specific runtime and to learn about how to add additional packages to a distroless container.

**Important notes:**
- This requires Docker 17.05 or higher.
- The dockerfile is assumed to be at the root level where the docker build command is run.
- Additionally, the dockerfile assumes that there is also a nodejs project at the root level with the following files: `package.json`, and a `server.js` file that sets up the web server and is invoked as follows: `"start": "node server.js"` from the `package.json` file. To see the content of `package.json` and `server.js`, see the section after the example below.

`1.` Write a multi-stage docker file:

    # Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation.
    # Licensed under the MIT License.
    FROM mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/base/nodejs:20 AS BASE

    WORKDIR /app

    COPY package*.json ./
    COPY server.js ./

    # Install app dependencies
    # which generates application artifacts needed to run the app
    RUN npm install

    # Install nodejs and its dependencies into a staging location
    # Staging directory is copied into the final distroless image
    RUN mkdir /staging \
        && tdnf install -y --releasever=3.0 --installroot /staging nodejs npm \
        && tdnf clean all \
        && rm -rf /staging/etc/dnf \
        && rm -rf /staging/run/* \
        && rm -rf /staging/var/cache/dnf \
        && find /staging/var/log -type f -size +0 -delete

    FROM mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/minimal:3.0 AS FINAL

    # Copy application build artifacts into the distroless container
    COPY --from=BASE /app .

    # Copy runtime dependencies into the distroless container
    COPY --from=BASE /staging/ .

    # Set the startup command for nodejs application
    CMD [ "npm", "run", "start" ]

`2.` Build and run your container image.

    docker build . -t distroless-nodejs-image
    docker run -p 8080:8080 --name distroless-nodejs-app -dt distroless-nodejs-image

`3.` Go to `localhost:8080` to see the nodejs server running.

#### Contents of package.json

    {
        "name": "node_app",
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "description": "Node.js app in Docker",
        "main": "server.js",
        "scripts": {
            "start": "node server.js"
        },
        "dependencies": {
            "express": "^4.19.2"
        }
    }

#### Contents of server.js

    'use strict';

    const express = require('express');

    // Constants
    const PORT = 8080;
    const HOST = '0.0.0.0';

    // App
    const app = express();
    app.get('/', (req, res) => {
      res.send('Hello from the node server running inside Azure Linux NodeJS distroless container.');
    });

    app.listen(PORT, HOST);
    console.log(`Running on http://${HOST}:${PORT}`);

## Usage

Depending on which Azure Linux version you want to use, replace `<image>` with one from the following: `minimal`, `base`, `debug` and replace `<tag>` with one from the Featured tags:

    docker run -it --rm mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/<image>:<tag>

For example,

    docker run -it --rm mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/minimal:3.0
    docker run -it --rm mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/base:3.0
    docker run -it --rm mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/distroless/debug:3.0

Note that distroless images by default do not contain a shell. So the above examples will not work as such. You can use docker's multi-stage build (defined in the Configuration section) to build and copy your application artifacts from a base image to distroless image and run your application.

## Support

Azure Linux container images are supported only for internal Microsoft use. For more information please see our [Support Statement](https://github.com/microsoft/azurelinux/blob/-/SUPPORT.md).
